documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION




Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.                             Docket No. ER26-3552-000




                    PROTEST OF COMMUNITY ORGANIZATIONS AND
                            CLEAN ENERGY ADVOCATES



    I.   INTRODUCTION

      Community Organizations1 and Clean Energy Advocates2 and their respective members reside

throughout the Midcontinent Independent System Operator Inc.’s (“MISO”) footprint. They rely

on MISO to provide affordable and reliable wholesale service to power many aspects of their lives,

including their residences, businesses, hospitals, places of worship, and schools. Their members

also rely on MISO’s adherence to non-discriminatory practices that enable a diverse set of energy

generation technologies, namely distributed energy resources, to provide low-cost energy options

that will help lower their energy bills without increasing pollution in their communities.

Additionally, one of Clean Energy Advocates is an organization including energy project

developers that regularly use MISO’s interconnection services.




1
 Community Organizations are Community Collaboration on Climate Change and Michigan Environmental Justice
Coalition, which are nonprofit organizations chartered under the laws of Michigan; and Midwest Tribal Energy
Resources Association, a nonstock corporation chartered under the laws of Wisconsin.
2
 Clean Energy Advocates consist of Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council, which are nonprofit
environmental organizations with members throughout MISO territory; and Clean Grid Alliance, a nonprofit
corporation chartered under the laws of Minnesota.


                                                       1
     On June 18, 2026, the Commission issued an order to show cause (“OSC” or “Show Cause

Order”) to MISO and its transmission owners (“TOs”) directing them to either provide more

options to fast track the grid interconnection of large load customers, which at the moment are

primarily data centers, or explain why MISO’s tariff is sufficient. MISO submitted its Zero

Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement (“ZGIA”) proposal (the “Proposal”) to respond to

the co-location requirements in the Commission’s OSC.3 Our organizations do not oppose the

intended design of MISO’s ZGIA Proposal—a co-location arrangement that results in no injections

or withdrawals of electrons to MISO’s transmission system and, therefore, does not require

network upgrades nor cause negative impacts to the Definitive Planning Phase (“DPP”) process.

Rather, we oppose the lack of processes and tariff provisions to make those design elements a

reality.

    Without proper tariff provisions, this process could have the opposite of MISO’s intended

effect by instead operationalizing ongoing cost shifts that will be difficult, if not impossible, for

states to untangle, triggering otherwise preventable reliability shortalls, and allowing generators

with ZGIA service (“ZG Resource”) to perpetually gain an unfair advantage over projects in DPP,

frustrating the implementation of Order 2023’s queue reforms to the detriment of market

participants and consumers, like our members. As discussed below, we urge the Commission to

direct MISO to address these tariff and procedural defects through either a deficiency letter or

direct further compliance via the show cause proceeding.




3
 Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Op., Inc.’s Transmittal Letter for Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement
Filing, Docket No. ER26-3552-000 (Aug. 18, 2026), Accession No. 20260818-5152 (“MISO Transmittal” or
“Transmittal Letter”).

    II.      ARGUMENT

             A. The Proposal Fails to Actually Ensure Zero Injection by ZG Generators.
                     1.      ZG Generating Facilities that Make Unauthorized Injections Should Be
                             Penalized.
       Zero injection is an extremely clear program design element in this Proposal,4 but MISO fails

to ensure that zero means zero. The Transmittal Letter, testimony, and proposed tariff language

are silent about what happens when a ZG Generator exports power to the grid outside the Point of



4
  Transmittal Letter at 8 (MISO stating that the “new generator with ZGIA Interconnection Service cannot inject past
the interconnecting substation…”); id at 13 (MISO stating that the “ZG Interconnection Service is limited to
requesting and being awarded Interconnection Service at a level that does not exceed the peak demand of the ZG
Associated Load.”


                                                                        3
 Interconnection (“POI”) and the Transient Tolerance Window. Yet the Commission clearly stated

in the Show Cause Order that it is concerned with the lack of tariff provisions that “specify

requirements for necessary control technologies and protections systems” needed to limit

withdrawals consistent with study arrangements and related agreements.5 The Commission should

require MISO to modify its ZGIA proposal to include robust operational penalties for ZGIA

Generating Facilities that make unauthorized injections into the MISO transmission system

notwithstanding the use of control technologies and/or protection systems.6 MISO cannot be silent

on its enforcement procedures in light of the serious reliability risks to the grid that may arise if a

ZGIA Generating Facility fails to limit its injections as promised. The Commission should require

MISO to impose strict operational penalties to give ZG Generating Facilities adequate incentives

to limit their injections as expected or risk termination of their transmission service if they fail to

perform.

                       i. Unauthorized injections are likely to increase reliability risks in MISO.

       Unauthorized injections on the transmission system can lead to increased reliability risks,

making it imperative that generators are properly incentivized to follow zero-injection

requirements. MISO has acknowledged the reliability risks associated with large loads, including

the risk associated with frequency and voltage instability, system balancing, and Area Control

Error volatility.7 MISO’s Board previously made a commitment to address the operational risks

associated with large loads, particularly with respect to ramping, adequacy, and stability.8 Yet, in




5
 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal
Power Act, 195 FERC ¶ 61,212, P 64 (2026).
6
    See generally, PJM Interconnection LLC, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 212 (2025) (“PJM Co-location Order”).
7
 Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System, Comments of the Midcontinent Independent
System Operator, Inc., Docket No. RM26-4-000, Accession No. 20251121-5472 at 30 (Nov. 21, 2025).
8
    Id. at 29, n.29.


                                                        4
 this filing, MISO fails to adequately address the severity of potential reliability issues that could

be caused by unauthorized injections on the system.

       Recent grid fluctuation events illustrate the serious reliability risks that could result from

unplanned injections on the system. In July 2026, over three GW of data centers on the PJM grid

suddenly disconnected, causing voltage and frequency fluctuations that could be detected from

Virginia to Illinois.9 While operators can typically correct grid disturbances within milliseconds,

this event took almost 10 minutes to stabilize.10 A similar event occurred two years prior, also in

PJM, where 1.5 GW of data center load suddenly dropped in Northern Virginia, forcing operators

to make emergency adjustments to prevent cascading outages.11 There is growing concern from

the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) about the increased amount of

customer initiated load reduction events as large, extended fluctuations can lead to cascading

fluctuations and system blackouts.12

       The Commission should require MISO to impose strict operational penalties to prevent similar

grid fluctuation events from occurring in MISO’s territory. MISO anticipates that ZG Associated

Loads may, at some point, suddenly decrease their load.13 The ZGIA proposal establishes a

Transient Tolerance Window during which the ZGIA Generating Facility will ramp down to match

playing-catch-up.

  Tim McLaughlin, Massive Disconnect of Power Roils Largest US Electric Grid, Reuters (Jul. 22, 2026),
https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/massive-disconnect-power-roiled-largest-us-electric-grid-2026-07-22.

electric-grid.
12

https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/who-we-are/standing-committees/rstc/whitepaper-characteristics-and-risks-of-

Commissioning, Operations, Protection, and Control (May 4, 2026),
https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/programs/bpsa/alerts/level-3-computational-load-alert.pdf, at 8.
13
     Transmittal Letter at 21.


                                                           5
 the reduced load level.14 MISO’s filing acknowledges that ZG Generating Facilities cannot

instantaneously ramp down to meet the associated load loss, which presents increased risks of grid

fluctuations as ZGIA arrangements attempt to stabilize. If multiple ZG Generating Facilities fail

to ramp down as expected, either by choice or by misoperation of control technology, the MISO

grid could experience cascading fluctuations across its system. As demonstrated in PJM, as more

GWs of load drop from the system, fluctuations are harder to manage. If MISO anticipates that

large loads will use the ZGIA service to connect to the grid, it must ensure that ZG Generating

Facilities will limit their injections when necessary. The control equipment and management

measures contemplated in the Proposal, even if optimally chosen,15 are not sufficient.

                         ii. Strong Operational Penalties Are Needed to Ensure That ZG Resources
                             Will Not Make Unauthorized Injections That Could Lead to Greater
                             Reliability Risks.

       The Commission must require MISO to implement strong penalties to prevent ZG Resources

from making unauthorized injections into MISO’s transmission system above their authorized

level of service (namely, zero), consistent with the Commission’s prior finding that transmission

customers should be subject to penalties for unreserved use of the transmission system.16 Absent

such penalties, the Proposal cannot be found just and reasonable.

       MISO’s ZGIA proposal fails to discuss any penalties to be levied on ZGIA Generating

Facilities that violate the rule against unauthorized injections outside the Transient Tolerance

Window.17 Similarly, MISO’s proposal states that the ZG Interconnection Service Study must




14
     Id.
15
  As discussed infra in section II.A.2, MISO has not optimally or adequately structured its requirements for control
equipment and measures.
16
   PJM Co-location Order at P 212 (2025) (directing PJM to brief appropriate penalty charges for transmission
customers’ unreserved use of the PJM transmission system).
17
     Transmittal Letter at 43.


                                                         6
 confirm that a generator’s proposed equipment can sufficiently limit injections, but is silent as to

any consequences if the equipment malfunctions and allows the generator to inject into the

transmission system outside the Transient Tolerance Window.18

       The Proposal contains no specific penalty schedule or mandatory reporting of injection events

and control failures. There seems to be no consequence for an unauthorized injection—no charge,

curtailment, suspension, mandatory retesting, or graduated penalty. This lackadaisical approach

to enforcement is inconsistent with the serious reliability risks that would occur if ZG Generating

Facilities made unauthorized injections into the system. When faced with potential consequences

as serious as widespread outages, MISO must implement operational penalties that are just as

serious.

       The Commission has already found that operational and financial penalties are just and

reasonable to ensure that customers follow curtailment directives, especially where there are

significant reliability risks if customers fail to curtail.19 In its recent proceeding on co-location

arrangements in PJM, the Commission directed PJM to establish an appropriate penalty charge

and “any other remedial action” that PJM should take to address a customer’s unreserved use of

the transmission system or excess energy withdrawals.20 PJM established three separate penalties

that escalated in severity based on the potential harm to the transmission system—a pause in

service, disqualification, and financial penalties—where customers rely on control technologies

that fail more than once, fail to follow Load Shedding and Curtailment directives, or make




18
     Transmittal Letter at 13, 14.
19
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Order on Rehearing, Clarification, Compliance Filing, and Paper Hearing, 195
FERC ¶ 61,209, at P 515 (2026) (“PJM Co-Location Rehearing Order”).
20
     PJM Co-location Order at P 212.


                                                       7
 unreserved use of the transmission system.21 The Commission found that it was just and

reasonable to establish these operational penalties because (1) PJM’s new services for co-location

arrangements were designed for Eligible Customers that are willing and able to limit their

withdrawals from the transmission system; and (2) there are significant reliability risks if Eligible

Customers fail to curtail.22

       Similarly, MISO’s ZGIA proposal is designed on the assumption that ZGIA Generation

Facilities can and will limit their injections on the system and that (like in PJM), there are serious

reliability risks if ZGIA Generating Facilities fail to limit their injections when directed to. MISO’s

proposal states that “[t]he premise of ZG Interconnection Service is that injections beyond the

interconnecting substation can be limited.”23 ZG Generating Facilities, and their ZG Associated

Loads, would be allowed to interconnect quickly on the assumption that they will adhere to strict

limitations on injections.24 Under the proposed ZG Interconnection Agreement, a Generating

Facility taking ZG Interconnection Service agrees to the requirements to install equipment to

reduce its injections at times when the ZG Associated Load reduces its demand and to cease all

injections onto the transmission system when necessary.25 Allowing ZGIA Generating Facilities

to connect quickly through ZGIA on the basis that they will limit their injections, but not enforcing

any penalties against them when they fail to limit those injections would, as PJM said with respect

to its co-location penalties filing, “implicitly bless such dangerous behavior.”26




21
  Initial Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-49-000, at 50 (Feb. 23, 2026), Accession No.
20260223-5189 (“PJM Initial Brief”).
22
     PJM Co-Location Rehearing Order at P 515.
23
     Transmittal Letter at 42.
24
     Transmittal Letter at 7.
25

26

        MISO should terminate or pause a ZG Generating Facility’s ability to use the transmission

system if the generator fails to stay true to its promise to limit its injections. Otherwise, ZGIA

Generating Facilities would receive the benefits of connecting to the grid quickly without

providing a commensurate benefit to the grid, and at worst, would risk endangering the stability

of the transmission system. The failure of a ZG Generating Facility to limit its injections could

cause reliability risks similar to those contemplated in PJM’s Co-Location docket, including a

higher risk of widespread outages across the bulk power system.27 In order to ensure that the

severe risks of failing to limit injections are weighed equally to the benefits that ZGIA Generation

Facilities receive from the ZG Interconnection Service, the Commission should require MISO to

impose operational penalties on Generating Facilities that fail to limit their injections as directed.

                   2.     ZGIA’s Requirement for System Protection Facilities is Poorly Defined.
       Next, MISO falls short in its unnecessarily weak standard for System Protection Facilities that

will ensure zero injection. The applicant ZG Generating Facility is required to identify “any

proposed system protection facilities”28 in its Interconnection Request. Although not capitalized

in that passage, System Protection Facilities is an existing defined term meaning, as relevant,

“equipment [] required to protect [] the Transmission System or other delivery systems or other

generating systems from faults or other electrical disturbances occurring at the Generating

Facility.”29 It is apparent from the filing that “System Protection Facilities” (or system protection

facilities) in this context is intended to “control injection onto the rest of the Transmission




27
   NERC, Characteristics and Risks of Emerging Large Loads: Large Loads Task Force White Paper, supra note 12,
at 20.
28
     Proposed Att. X § 3.11(ii); Att. X, App’x 1 § 10 and Att. A-5.
29

                                                                9
 System,”30 although that is not codified in the proposed tariff. Following the Interconnection

Request, the proposed ZG Facilities Study is to identify “any required system protection facilities

and equipment,”31 with such facilities memorialized in the ZG Interconnection Agreement.32

       MISO’s proposal falls short of what is needed to ensure that zero means zero by missing any

minimum configuration of System Protection Facilities necessary to block unauthorized power

injections to the grid beyond the POI. Outside the proposed tariff, MISO narrates its intentions:

           “MISO anticipates reviewing a variety of configurations, physical equipment, and
           operational requirements that may independently, or in sum, prevent injections on
           the Transmission System beyond the substation where the Point of Interconnection
           is located. For example, the injection limitation may be implemented through
           equipment controls such as export-limiting controls, directional relays, interlocks,
           and fail-safe trip logic. Operational requirements may include generation limits,
           curtailment obligations, outage coordination, and restrictions on operation. These
           operational requirements are in addition to any monitoring, testing, or maintenance
           requirements.”33

       The lack of clarity with this choose-your-own-adventure configuration approach is precisely

why the Commission directed transmission providers to submit tariff proposals or explain why

they are not needed.34 No export-limiting control device (nor control over such device) is

required anywhere in the proposed tariff. MISO proposes to give itself discretion to judge

whether the “proposed control equipment and/or operating procedures […] are sufficient to

prevent injections”35 (emphasis added), suggesting that a protocol for manual intervention alone

 by the ZG Generating Facility’s operator might be acceptable to MISO. The Commission in the

Show Cause Order called for MISO to develop generator interconnection service that reflects “a

generating facility with necessary control technologies and/or protection systems, which may

include a special protection scheme, that ensure that the injection does not exceed the limit in the

[…] interconnection agreement.”36 “Special protection scheme” was defined there as in the PJM

Co-Location Rehearing Order,37 which in turn referenced the PJM Co-Location Order: “a plan

designed to detect abnormal system conditions and to automatically take appropriate corrective

action, to maintain system stability, acceptable system voltages, and acceptable facility

loading”38 (emphasis added). But, defying the Commission’s directives, MISO here proposes no

requirement for automatic corrective action.

       Additionally, the Proposal fails to be just and reasonable in missing any specific requirements

for testing the protective measures. The ZG Interconnection Agreement gives MISO a “right to

inspect” the ZG Generating Facility’s “System Protection Facilities and other protective

equipment,” including looking at tests, inspections, settings, and maintenance records, but sets

no requirement for MISO to do so at any particular interval.39 Similarly, the agreement requires

the ZG Generating Facility to test its System Protection Facilities “[a]t intervals suggested by

Good Utility Practice” but does not set any interval or require MISO to verify the testing.40 This

stands in contrast to, for example, the clear requirement for a ZG Generating Facility’s metering

equipment to be testified at least biennially.41

                   3.     Length of the Transient Tolerance Window Should be Set According to
                         Clear Standards.
       A third infirmity in ensuring that zero means zero is how MISO proposes to set the “Transient

Tolerance Window,” which is “the period of time after a reduction or loss of load by the ZG

Associated Load by the end of which window the [ZG] Generating Facility must have” ceased

injections to the grid.42 In other words, this time span, defined as no more than 20 seconds,43 is

the time for a ZG Generating Facility to ramp down production as needed when its co-located load

drops. This time window is a fundamental engineering parameter of ZGIA service, but MISO has

not justified why a maximum period of 20 seconds is either operationally attainable by a generator

(or if a greater or lesser time window would be more appropriate), or operationally acceptable for

the transmission grid to remain stably within reliability criteria while receiving unexpected

injections over that time interval.

       MISO states that it “determined that a 20-second limit provides the best system-wide balance

between what is technically feasible and commercially practical on the one hand, and minimizing

even transient injections on the other hand”;44 and MISO’s witness Keyser opines that 20 seconds

was chosen “in order to align with the MTEP modeling interval of 20 seconds for transient stability

analysis.”45 The physical or even customary basis of 20 seconds remains obscure, as this figure is

mentioned neither in the existing Attachment FF (Transmission Expansion Planning Protocol) nor

in Business Practices Manual 20 (Transmission Planning). MISO should better justify the specific

time interval chosen with reference to NERC standards, local planning criteria, or some other

grounding in electrical engineering realities.



42
     Proposed Att. X § 1; proposed Att. X, App’x 19, Art. 1 (proposed definition of Transient Tolerance Window).
43
     Id.
44
     Transmittal Letter at 21-22.
45
     Keyser Test. at 25:20-22


                                                          12
        An additional deficiency with MISO’s definition of Transient Tolerance Window is its

allowance that 20 seconds would be the maximum period allowed, while the time period could be

“further described by the Business Practices Manual for Large Load.”46 MISO gives more color

its intentions in its filing letter, offering that “there may be circumstances where a narrower

window is necessary and practical given electrical topography on certain parts of the MISO

System, or Applicable Local Planning Criteria. It would be impractical to identify all such

circumstances in the Tariff. Therefore, the definition allows for the creation of Business Practices

Manual (“BPM”) rules that narrow the window based on specific circumstances[.]”47 A tariff that

remained silent about all the standards and intentions in the prior quotation while reserving

authority for MISO to make discretionary changes outside the Commission’s oversight would

violate the Rule of Reason, which requires that provisions that (1) significantly affect rates, terms,

and conditions of service, (2) are realistically susceptible of specification, and are (3) not generally

understood in a contractual agreement must be included in the tariff.48 While the D.C. Circuit has

recently recognized that “even specifiable practices that significantly affect rates need not be

included if they are clearly implied by the tariff’s express terms,”49 the proposed tariff’s passing

reference to the BPM hardly implies anything as to how MISO will consider varying the 20-second

rule.

       As a policy matter, users of ZGIA service, not to mention regulators and stakeholders, will

want to develop reasonable expectations about how the 20-second interval for unauthorized

injections might evolve; but the placement of untariffed policies in the Business Practices Manual

 will complicate that. A Transient Tolerance Window that MISO can adjust by standardless fiat

hardly supports orderly market development.

            B. The Proposal Lacks Required Transparency.

       The Commission found in the Show Cause Order that MISO must provide “cost transparency

measures […] to provide stakeholders with sufficient information and visibility regarding the

Network Upgrades, and their associated costs, needed to provide transmission service to Eligible

Customers on behalf of large loads.”50 The Commission further found that MISO’s tariff is not

just and reasonable to the extent “it does not require the provision of data on MISO’s website in a

single location, and in an easily accessible format that is searchable and allows users to filter the

data, that identifies the Network Upgrades that are needed to accommodate requests for

transmission service by Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads, and the costs of those Network

Upgrades.”51 Despite this clear command from the Commission for transparency of large load52-

induced costs, and MISO’s stated attempt to respond to the Show Cause Order, MISO has fallen

well short of the Order’s clear requirements on transparency. It is simply not correct that the

“ZGIA proposal is well aligned with the Commission’s goals and objectives of transparency,” as

MISO avers.53




50
     Show Cause Order at P 71.
51
     Id. P 77.
52
  Although the ZGIA proposal is not restricted to serving only large loads, it is reasonable to expect that large loads
will be a significant share of the end-use customers benefiting from the program. “MISO notes that this description
[generally outlining ZGIA] explains how ZGIA will serve large loads”; “The ZGIA proposal represents another
critical tool to help support the timely, reliable, cost-effective integration of new large loads into the MISO system”;
“the ZGIA is particularly responsive to the needs of a large load[.]” Transmittal Letter at 8 n.33, 9, 11.
53
     Transmittal Letter at 5.


                                                          14
        MISO is aware of how to design an interconnection program with deliberate transparency, as

the Commission found last year.54 Yet, no provision within the ZGIA proposal requires MISO to

post ZGIA study reports, required Network Upgrades identified or deferred, or affected-system

results. No provision requires the publication of costs of such upgrades, once known. Without the

underlying studies and upgrade information, stakeholders and regulators may be unable to quantify

incremental costs attributable to an expedited project or evaluate whether later MTEP upgrades

result from assumptions made in the ZGIA process. The existing generator interconnection tariff

includes various precedents55 for required publication of data, and there is no reason why MISO

could not post vital information on Network Upgrades.

       MISO may rest on its requirement that a ZG Generating Facility can qualify for ZG

Interconnection Service only if the ZG Impact Assessment and ZG Facilities Study find that the

proposed interconnection “[w]ill not require the construction or modification of any Network

Upgrades to address impacts to the Transmission System with the exception of Network Upgrades

located at the same substation as the POI, except for System Protection Facilities at adjacent

substations.”56 However, to the extent the ZG Generating Facility is owned by a vertically

integrated, state-regulated utility, the costs of Network Upgrades, even if borne by the generator’s

utility owner, may be allocated in indeterminate ways at the retail level. The ZG studies may also

identify foregone Network Upgrades that would have been required to interconnect the generator

absent the ZG Associated Load, or Network Upgrades that would have been required to

accommodate the new load absent the ZG Generating Facility. It will be important to track these

publicly post detailed information about each ERAS interconnection request and its corresponding type of load
served”).
55

56
     Proposed Att. X § 3.2.5.1(2); also see §§ 3.2.5.2.1, 3.2.5.2.2, 3.11(iii).

 foregone upgrades should either the ZG Associated Load or ZG Generating Facility depart the co-

located arrangement in the future, putting upgrade costs back on the table. Overall, the Proposal

falls well short of the necessary transparency urged by the Commission.

            C. The ZGIA Program’s Scope Should Have a Defined Limitation.

       The Commission’s two orders last year on the ERAS fast-track interconnection program

emphasized the Commission’s longstanding policy on open access to the transmission system and

requirement to limit the scope of departures therefrom. The first ERAS order denied MISO’s

initial proposal as not just and reasonable, in part because it lacked a program size cap (in either

project counts or project megawatts).57 The Commission also found that the proposed program

end date of December 2028, allowing for three and a half years’ worth of project selections, would

“exacerbate[] the potential for a volume of ERAS interconnection requests untethered to reliability

or resource adequacy needs” and would “make[] it difficult to determine […] whether the solution

        D. The Proposal Fails to Adequately Mitigate the Risk that Network Upgrades Will
           Be Paid by Other than the Cost Causers.

     MISO’s ZGIA proposal includes two primary mechanisms that together are designed to prevent

cost-shifting from ZGIA projects to other interconnection customers or load. These mechanisms

involve: 1) a requirement that, in order to qualify for ZG Interconnection Service to begin with,

the ZG Generating Facility will not require additional large-scale network upgrades, and 2) that

MISO can credit the ZG Generating Facility as a “Non-Transmission Alternative” as a result of

signing five-year commitments with ZGIA load. However, as further described below, those

protective measures do not sufficiently insulate Network Upgrade costs from instances when some

or all the ZG Associated Load is not placed in service.

     Specifically, as discussed in section II.D.2 below, there are at least three principal flaws with

the Proposal that can result in cost-shifting: 1) the five-year commitment is insufficiently concrete

to provide the requisite certainty that the load integration study and its assumptions regarding

needed upgrades are accurate; 2) the structure of the Proposal creates a fast-track ZGIA to GIA

process whereby ZG Generating Facility could later convert to ERIS or NRIS service and thereby

III.      CONCLUSION

   To effectuate MISO’s zero injection concept without raising the risk of adverse reliability

events and cost shifts, Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates respectfully ask the

Commission to use its authority to help MISO course correct. Given the demonstrated reliability

concerns interconnecting and serving large load customers, no countervailing reasons justify

failing to establish operational penalties and transparent baseline requirements for system

protection mechanisms.     Similarly, as the Commission noted in the OSC, cost transparency is

paramount given the scale and pace of forecasted load growth. Without publishing study

information and reducing instances for mismatching cost responsibility between the multiple

generator interconnection queue processes, MISO’s ZGIA process could unduly shift cost burdens

to other ratepayers without giving states and other advocates visibility to identify or resolve the

issues.
